questions.q: What is the most common reason a data governance program stalls in its first year, according to this lesson?
options: A readiness gap — missing sponsorship, capacity, or business agreement — not a lack of technology
The catalog tool chosen was the wrong vendor
The program moved too slowly through its roadmap phases
There were too many data stewards assigned
questions.explain: Teams often buy tooling and write a charter while skipping the readiness check — the real gap is almost always sponsorship, capacity, or business agreement, not the technology.

questions.q: Why should each readiness dimension be rated independently rather than averaged into one overall score?
options: Because an organization can be strong in one dimension and weak in another, and that combination is itself meaningful information
Because averaging is mathematically impossible with Low/Medium/High ratings
Because only the technology dimension actually matters
Because regulators require dimensions to be scored separately
questions.explain: High regulatory pressure with low sponsorship tells you something very different than the reverse — averaging the two into one number would erase that signal.

questions.q: Why does an assessment run entirely by the IT department fall short?
options: It produces a technology inventory rather than a true readiness assessment, since most of the dimensions are about people and process
IT staff are not allowed to participate in governance assessments
It takes longer than a business-led assessment
It always overstates regulatory pressure
questions.explain: Sponsorship, current practices, and organizational structure are business-side realities — an IT-only assessment tends to rate them too generously because it never leaves the IT org.

questions.q: What is a 'gap list' in the context of a readiness assessment?
options: A prioritized output listing each dimension's current rating, target rating, and the gap between them
A list of employees who have not completed governance training
A record of data quality defects found during the assessment
The set of policies still missing from the policy library
questions.explain: The gap list translates raw observations into something actionable — current state vs. target state per dimension — and directly feeds the business case and pilot selection.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified in this lesson as a readiness-assessment trap?
options: Treating the assessment as a one-time event instead of repeating it after major organizational change
Rating too many dimensions instead of too few
Involving too many business stakeholders in the assessment
Running the assessment before choosing an operating model
questions.explain: Readiness changes over time — a merger, a leadership change, or a new regulation can shift the picture, so the assessment should be revisited, not treated as permanent.
